title: How fast does a square grow?

beats.text: Here is a square, three units on each side. Its area is nine: nine little unit squares.
Now stretch each side by just one tenth. How much area did we add? Make a guess before we look.
The new area comes in three pieces: a strip along the top, a strip down the side, and one tiny corner.
Each strip is three long and one tenth thin, so each adds three tenths. The corner is a tenth by a tenth, just one hundredth.
Add them up, and the area grew by sixty one hundredths. Almost all of it came from the two strips.
Now make the nudge smaller, and watch what happens to each piece.
The strips shrink in step with the nudge. But the corner shrinks far faster, because it is small in both directions. Up close, it is barely a speck.
So ask a sharper question. How much new area do we get for each bit of nudge? Divide each row's new area by its nudge.
The answer closes in on six. And six is simply the two strips, each three long.
Nothing here depended on the side being three. Change the side, and the answer follows along: always two times the side.
Each strip is exactly as long as the side. So for every bit of nudge, you gain two sides' worth of new area.
Let's write down what we found, in plain words first. The new area, divided by the nudge, is about two times the side.
Mathematicians like short names. The side usually gets called x.
The nudge is a tiny change in the side, so we write it with a little d in front.
And the new area is a tiny change in the square's area. So it gets the same little d.
Now let the nudge shrink all the way to nothing. The corner vanishes, the approximation becomes exact, and the result has a name: the derivative.
Plug in a side of three, and out comes six, exactly what the strips told us.
So this formula is not a rule to memorize. It is a picture: two edges where new area appears. Try the same idea on a growing cube.
